\chapter{In the House}
\label{ch:te-house}
\hlchaptermodality{56}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five ordinary things inside a Telugu house and thank somebody for handing me one.}

\section[cāpa]{\te{చాప} (cāpa) — a mat}

\label{lesson:TE-C56-mat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bāṭa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చాప}}
\textbf{\te{చాప}} (\emph{cāpa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a mat\textquotedblright{}.

A \te{చాప} is woven from palm leaf or reed, rolled up against a wall by day and unrolled to sit or sleep on.

It belongs beside the \te{కుర్చీ} you already have. Where the chair is a borrowed thing with a borrowed name, the \te{చాప} is old and the word is inherited, and a house that has both will often put the \te{చాప} down for the people who are comfortable on the floor and keep the \te{కుర్చీ} for the guest who is not.

Offering somebody a \te{చాప} is an invitation to stay a while. It is a slower gesture than pointing at a chair.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first thing a floor gets.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cāpa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cāpa}, then \emph{kurcī}, and say which of the two gets rolled up
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చాప} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a mat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[buṭṭa]{\te{బుట్ట} (buṭṭa) — a basket}

\label{lesson:TE-C56-basket}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cāpa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{బుట్ట}}
\textbf{\te{బుట్ట}} (\emph{buṭṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a basket\textquotedblright{}.

\te{బుట్ట} is inherited: the woven basket that carries vegetables home, holds flowers for the morning, and sits on a head on the way to market.

Weaving words tend to be old, and they tend to stay put while the trade words move around them. A \te{బుట్ట} and a \te{చాప} come off the same hands and the same palm leaf, which is why the two words feel like family even though they are not.

\te{పూల} \te{బుట్ట} is the flower basket — \te{పువ్వు}'s \te{పూల}- shape doing its work again.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: something to sit on, something to carry with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{buṭṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{buṭṭa}, then \emph{cāpa}, and say what the two are made of
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{బుట్ట} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a basket\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[katti]{\te{కత్తి} (katti) — a knife}

\label{lesson:TE-C56-knife}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{buṭṭa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కత్తి}}
\textbf{\te{కత్తి}} (\emph{katti}) — \textquotedblleft{}a knife\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కత్తి} is the knife and, in older use, the sword. Size did not divide them; the blade did.

It is inherited, and it is spread right across the family — Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam all have a word of the same shape for a cutting blade. Tools that a household could make for itself keep their names for a very long time.

\te{కత్తి} also does the work English gives to \textquotedblleft{}sharp\textquotedblright{} when talking about people: \te{కత్తిలాంటి} is knife-like, said of somebody quick.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{katti}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{katti}, then \emph{buṭṭa}, and say which one you would cut a \te{పండు} with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కత్తి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a knife\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ginne]{\te{గిన్నె} (ginne) — a cooking vessel, a bowl}

\label{lesson:TE-C56-vessel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{katti} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గిన్నె}}
\textbf{\te{గిన్నె}} (\emph{ginne}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cooking vessel, a bowl\textquotedblright{}.

\te{గిన్నె} is the round metal vessel that food is cooked and served in — the everyday one, brass or steel, with no lid worth mentioning.

Telugu splits its containers finely. A \te{గిన్నె} is not a \te{కుండ}, the fired clay pot, and it is not a \te{పళ్ళెం}, the flat plate. English pushes all three towards \textquotedblleft{}pot\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}dish\textquotedblright{} and loses the difference between what holds heat, what holds water and what holds a meal.

When a kitchen has a name for each shape, the names are telling you which shapes the kitchen actually uses.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ginne}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ginne}, then \emph{katti}, and say which one goes on the fire
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గిన్నె} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a cooking vessel, a bowl\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[peṭṭe]{\te{పెట్టె} (peṭṭe) — a box}

\label{lesson:TE-C56-box}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ginne} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పెట్టె}}
\textbf{\te{పెట్టె}} (\emph{peṭṭe}) — \textquotedblleft{}a box\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పెట్టె} comes straight out of \te{పెట్టు}, \textquotedblleft{}to put\textquotedblright{}: the box is the put-place. Telugu builds a good many of its household words this way, from the thing you do to the thing you do it in.

Then the railways arrived and \te{పెట్టె} picked up a second job — a railway carriage is a \te{పెట్టె}, a box that people are put in. A word for putting things away ended up on the side of a train.

The house is furnished now: a \te{చాప} on the floor, a \te{బుట్ట} by the door, a \te{కత్తి} and a \te{గిన్నె} in the kitchen, and a \te{పెట్టె} for what is not needed today.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{చాప}, \te{బుట్ట}, \te{కత్తి}, \te{గిన్నె}, \te{పెట్టె}. You can name what a room holds, and say \te{ధన్యవాదాలు} when one is handed to you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{peṭṭe}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then take one from somebody and say \emph{dhanyavādālu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పెట్టె} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a box\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
